planting.note: Plant dormant or containerized stock in spring after the ground has thawed and worked, in a site with good drainage.

directions: A compact hybrid of Deutzia gracilis and D. parviflora, 'Boule de Neige' produces dense, rounded clusters of small white star-shaped flowers that smother the branches in early summer, giving the plant its snowball nickname. Growth is tidy and upright with fine-textured, opposite leaves and attractive flaking bark on older wood. Prune immediately after flowering, removing a portion of the oldest canes at ground level to keep the plant renewing itself. Tolerates average garden soil once established and needs little supplemental care beyond occasional deep watering in drought.

planting.note: Set out container stock in spring; this early-blooming species sets its flower buds on old wood so avoid hard fall pruning.

directions: Weigela praecox is the earliest-blooming of the weigelas, opening its rosy-pink, yellow-throated, fragrant flowers one to two weeks ahead of the common Weigela florida cultivars. The 'Variegata' selection adds cream-white leaf margins that brighten the shrub through the growing season after the spring flower show fades. It forms a rounded, multi-stemmed mound and benefits from renewal pruning of the oldest canes right after flowering. Give it full sun for the best variegation contrast and heaviest bloom.

planting.note: Install bare-root or container plants in early spring; this is one of the first spireas to leaf out and bloom.

directions: A hybrid of Spiraea cana and S. hypericifolia, 'Grefsheim' is among the earliest spireas to flower, lining its slender gray-green, gracefully arching branches with small white blooms in very early spring, often before the narrow leaves fully unfurl. The fine, airy texture and fountain-like habit distinguish it from the coarser, later-blooming bridal wreath types. It is extremely cold-hardy and tolerates lean, dry soils once established. Rejuvenate by thinning out a few of the oldest stems right after bloom rather than shearing the whole plant.
sources: Scandinavian and North American nursery references

planting.note: Transplant in early spring or fall into a sunny border; flower buds form the prior summer, so prune only right after bloom.

directions: This selection softens the typical bold forsythia gold to a pale, primrose-yellow, giving a more subdued early-spring display before the leaves emerge. Habit is the familiar upright, fountain-like forsythia shape with long arching canes well suited to informal hedges or a mixed border. Full sun produces the heaviest flowering; part shade reduces bloom density noticeably. Renewal-prune a third of the oldest stems to the ground every year or two to keep the shrub vigorous and well-shaped.

planting.note: Plant in spring in a site with some afternoon shade in hot climates, which helps preserve the cream variegation.

directions: The lance-shaped green leaves of this old-fashioned shrub are heavily splashed with creamy white, strongest on new growth and giving the whole plant a pale, frosted look from a distance. Clusters of fragrant white, star-shaped flowers appear in late spring to early summer along the upright, arching canes, with the rough-textured ('scabra') bark adding winter interest once leaves drop. In regions with hot summers the variegation tends to green up as temperatures climb, so afternoon shade helps hold the pattern longer. Remove the oldest flowering canes after bloom to maintain an open, graceful form.

planting.note: Set out in early spring; this is the classic double-flowered form sold in nurseries as 'bridal wreath'.

directions: Small, fully double white pompon-like flowers, each about a third of an inch across, line the bare, arching stems in tight clusters of three to six in early spring, well before the finely toothed leaves emerge. This double-flowered selection is the form almost always sold under the common name bridal wreath, as the single-flowered wild species is rarely offered. Fall color on the small dark-green leaves can turn orange to burgundy in a good year. Thin out the oldest wood right after flowering to keep the vase-shaped habit from becoming congested.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun for the heaviest flush of red flowers.

directions: 'Eva Supreme' bears funnel-shaped, true-red flowers in dense clusters along arching branches from late spring into early summer, with simple ovate green leaves that set off the bloom color well. It forms a broad, rounded mound larger than many modern compact weigela selections, making it a good choice for an informal flowering hedge or shrub border. Full sun gives the densest flowering and best branching habit. Prune to shape right after the main spring flush to encourage a second, lighter round of bloom later in the season.

planting.note: Plant in spring in well-drained soil; this low mounding deutzia also works well massed as a border edge.

directions: This Deutzia x rosea selection carries noticeably larger, bell-shaped flowers than typical forms of the cross, opening white flushed with pink in dense, profuse clusters along slender branches in late spring. The habit is low and mounding to gently arching, smaller in stature than the Deutzia scabra and x hybrida types, making it useful at the front of a shrub border. It tolerates a half-day of shade better than many deutzias and still flowers well. Thin out a portion of the oldest stems after bloom to keep new flowering wood coming on.

planting.note: Plant in spring; this vigorous, suckering hybrid spirea tolerates damp ground better than most spireas.

directions: Unlike the spring-blooming Spiraea japonica and vanhouttei types, this hybrid of S. douglasii and S. salicifolia flowers in summer, topping its upright canes with dense, narrow, erect panicles of bright rosy-pink blooms that resemble small bottlebrushes. The habit is vigorous and suckering, useful for naturalizing or stabilizing a bank where a tidy clump form isn't needed. It tolerates heavier, moisture-retentive soils better than most spireas thanks to its Spiraea douglasii parentage. Deadhead spent flower panicles to encourage additional summer bloom and divide or thin the colony periodically to control spread.
